\chapter{True, False, and Not Even}
\label{ch:verdad-y-siquiera}
\hlchaptermodality{324}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can weigh what somebody has told me with verdad, falso, acaso, menos and ni siquiera, and say which two Latin twins gave mas and menos.}

Complete ES-C324-siquiera: call a claim la verdad or falso, hedge it with acaso, size it with mas o menos, and empty it out with ni siquiera.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la verdad]{la verdad — the noun inside a question you already ask}

\label{lesson:ES-C324-verdad}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{afterwards}, then \emph{while}. (\emph{Después}; \emph{mientras}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ¿verdad? — the tag you already hang on the end of a sentence.
  \item -dad — the ending that answers to English \emph{-ty}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ver-DAD}, the weight on the second beat. The \emph{v} is soft, made without closing the lips, and the final \emph{-d} is softer still — closer to the \emph{th} of \emph{this}, and in much of the Spanish-speaking world it fades away entirely. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la verdad} — \textquotedblleft{}the truth.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{vērus} meant \emph{true}, and \textbf{vēritās} was the state of being so. The \emph{-tās} ending is the one you have met wearing Spanish clothes as \emph{-dad}: Latin \emph{-tātem} became Spanish \emph{-dad} and English \emph{-ty} out of the same starting point, which is why \emph{veritas} lands as both \textbf{verdad} and \textbf{verity}.

English carries the root in more places than it admits. To \textbf{verify} is to make true. \textbf{Veracity} is truthfulness. A \textbf{verdict} is \emph{vērē dictum} — \emph{truly said}, two Latin words a jury still hands over as one. And \emph{very} began as an adjective meaning \emph{true}: a \emph{very} fool once meant a \emph{true} fool, and only later did it drift into meaning \emph{extremely}.

You have been saying the Spanish word for a while without unpacking it. When you end a sentence with \textbf{¿verdad?} you are asking \emph{truth?} — \emph{is that the truth?} Now the noun stands on its own: \textbf{la verdad} is the thing itself, and \textbf{de verdad} means \emph{for real}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for weighing what somebody has told you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la verdad}
  \item \emph{de verdad}
  \item \emph{es la verdad, ¿verdad?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{vērus} mean? (True.) And what two Latin words are folded into English \emph{verdict}? (\emph{Vērē dictum} — truly said.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[falso]{falso — the opposite, and a word you have already met in the plural}

\label{lesson:ES-C324-falso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{while}, then \emph{the truth}. (\emph{Mientras}; \emph{la verdad}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item falsos amigos — you have already carried this word around in its plural.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FAL-so}, the weight on the first beat. The \emph{l} stays bright and forward, not swallowed the way an English \emph{l} goes dark before a consonant. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{falso} — \textquotedblleft{}false,\textquotedblright{} and often \textquotedblleft{}fake.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{fallere} meant \emph{to trip somebody up} — to make a foot go where the ground was not. \textbf{Falsus} was its past participle: \emph{tripped up}, and so \emph{deceived}, and so \emph{untrue}.

English collected the whole family and kept the pieces in different rooms. \textbf{False} is the participle, borrowed whole. To \textbf{fail} is \emph{fallere} through French — the ground giving way under you. A \textbf{fault} is where the ground did give way, in a person or in rock. A \textbf{fallacy} is an argument that trips you. Something \textbf{fallible} can be tripped.

Spanish kept the verb too, worn down to \textbf{faltar} — \emph{to be lacking} — so a thing that \emph{falta} is a thing that has let you down by not being there.

The ending moves, because \emph{falso} describes somebody or something: \emph{un billete falso}, \emph{una moneda falsa}. And you have met the plural already, in the name for words that look like English and lie about it — \textbf{falsos amigos}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two words, and between them a scale you can put any sentence on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{falso}
  \item \emph{verdad o falso}
  \item \emph{una moneda falsa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{fallere} do to you? (Tripped you up.) And which everyday English verb is the same word through French? (\emph{Fail}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acaso]{acaso — the third answer, when neither of the first two fits}

\label{lesson:ES-C324-acaso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the truth}, then \emph{false}. (\emph{La verdad}; \emph{falso}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item quizás and tal vez — two words for \emph{maybe} that you already have.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-CA-so}, three beats, the weight in the middle. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}, the same \emph{c} as in \emph{casa}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{acaso} — \textquotedblleft{}perhaps,\textquotedblright{} and underneath that, \emph{by chance}.

Break it and there are two pieces: \emph{a} and \emph{caso}. Latin \textbf{cāsus} was \emph{a falling}, from \textbf{cadere}, \emph{to fall} — and what falls, in Latin as in English, is dice. A \emph{cāsus} was how the dice landed. So \emph{a caso} is \emph{at the fall}, and to say something happens \emph{acaso} is to say it happens the way dice land.

The fall is everywhere in English. A \textbf{case} is how a matter has fallen out. A \textbf{casualty} is somebody the fall came down on. Something \textbf{casual} happens as it falls, without arrangement. A \textbf{cadence} is a falling line of sound. To \textbf{decay} is to fall away. An \textbf{accident} is \emph{ad-cadere}, a falling toward you. Even \emph{chance} is Latin \emph{cadentia}, \emph{a falling}, worn down through French.

Spanish already gave you \emph{quizás} and \emph{tal vez}. \textbf{Acaso} is the third, and it leans differently: dropped into a question — \emph{¿acaso no es verdad?} — it stops being \emph{maybe} and turns into a challenge, closer to English \emph{surely} said with a raised eyebrow.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
True, false, and the wide space between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{acaso}
  \item \emph{acaso es verdad}
  \item \emph{¿acaso es falso?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{cāsus} mean before it meant \emph{case}? (A falling — how the dice came down.) And what does \emph{acaso} do to a question? (Turns it into a challenge.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[menos]{menos — the other half of a pair you have been using one side of}

\label{lesson:ES-C324-menos}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{false}, then \emph{perhaps}. (\emph{Falso}; \emph{acaso}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item más que — the comparison you can already make in one direction.
  \item regular — the middling answer, built on this same root.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ME-nos}, the weight on the first beat. The final \emph{-s} is pronounced clearly across most of Latin America, and softens toward a breath in the Caribbean and southern Spain. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{menos} — \textquotedblleft{}less,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}fewer.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had a matched pair, and Spanish kept both: \textbf{magis} for the more of a thing and \textbf{minus} for the less. \emph{Magis} wore down into \emph{más}. \emph{Minus} barely moved at all — say \emph{minus} quickly and you have \emph{menos}.

English took the smaller twin without changing it either. \textbf{Minus} is the arithmetic. A \textbf{minor} matter is a smaller one. A \textbf{minimum} is the least. A \textbf{minute} was a \emph{pars minuta}, a made-small part of an hour, and the adjective \textbf{minute} meaning \emph{tiny} is the same word with its old stress. To \textbf{diminish} is to make less. And a \textbf{minister} was once \emph{minus}-plus-an-ending: the lesser one, the servant — the opposite number of a \emph{magister}, the greater one, who becomes the English \emph{master}.

Two everyday phrases carry it. \textbf{Más o menos} is \emph{more or less}, and it is the most common answer to \emph{¿cómo estás?} there is. \textbf{Por lo menos} is \emph{at least}. And \emph{menos} has a second job with no English echo: after a list, it means \emph{except}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A dial you can turn both ways, and the safest answer in the language.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{menos}
  \item \emph{más o menos}
  \item \emph{por lo menos, es verdad}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word gave \emph{más}, and which gave \emph{menos}? (\emph{Magis} and \emph{minus}.) And what was a \emph{minister} before it was a government job? (The lesser one — the servant.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[siquiera]{siquiera — a word made of two words you already own}

\label{lesson:ES-C324-siquiera}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{perhaps}, then \emph{more or less}. (\emph{Acaso}; \emph{más o menos}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item si — \emph{if}, without an accent.
  \item quiera · quieras · quiera — the \emph{wanting} form used for things that are not settled.
  \item ni — \emph{nor}, the word that will stand in front of it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{si-KYE-ra}, four beats with the weight on the third. The \emph{qu} is a plain \emph{k} with a silent \emph{u}, and \emph{ie} rides through as one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{siquiera} — \textquotedblleft{}even,\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}at least.\textquotedblright{}

Nothing new arrived. Spanish took \emph{si} and \emph{quiera} — both of them already yours — and pushed them together until they stopped being two words. \emph{Si quiera} meant \emph{if he should want it}, the shrug you make when the smallest version of something would do. Said often enough, the seam closed and the meaning thinned into \emph{even}.

The Latin underneath \emph{quiera} is \textbf{quaerere}, \emph{to seek}, and English kept the seeking rather than the wanting: to \textbf{query} is to seek an answer, to \textbf{acquire} is to seek toward, an \textbf{inquest} is a seeking-into, and a \textbf{quest} is the bare verb standing alone.

Two uses carry almost all of the weight. On its own, \textbf{siquiera} softens a request down to the smallest acceptable size: \emph{siquiera un poco} — \emph{at least a little}. With \textbf{ni} in front, it does the opposite and empties the sentence out: \textbf{ni siquiera} is \emph{not even}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words for weighing a claim: true, false, perhaps, less — and not even.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{siquiera}
  \item \emph{ni siquiera}
  \item \emph{siquiera un poco}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two words are welded together inside \emph{siquiera}? (\emph{Si} and \emph{quiera}.) And what does \emph{ni} in front of it do? (Makes it \emph{not even}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
